The Section on Further Exposition, Chapter Two: Convergence (Sampāta)
The Application of the Mode of Investigation: In this context, what is the application of the mode of investigation?
Herein, craving is twofold: both wholesome and unwholesome.
Unwholesome craving leads to saṃsāra, while wholesome craving leads to diminution and is to be abandoned.
Conceit is also twofold: wholesome and unwholesome.
That conceit by relying upon which one abandons conceit is wholesome.
Furthermore, that conceit which produces suffering is unwholesome.
In this regard, there arises for one a state of dejection based on renunciation, thinking:
"When shall I, having realized that base which the Noble Ones, having realized, enter and dwell in—that peaceful base? and so forth.
Envy; due to envy, there is grief. This is unwholesome craving. The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is wholesome;
the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance, which has that as its object, is wholesome.
What is the investigation of that?
The eight factors of the path are right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Where is this to be seen?
In the fourth jhāna of the perfection.

For in the fourth jhāna, he develops the mind endowed with eight factors—purified, bright, free from blemish, rid of secondary defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability.
Therein he attains eight things: the six direct knowledges and two distinctions. Because that mind is purified, it is bright;
because it is bright, it is free from blemish; because it is free from blemish, it is rid of secondary defilements.
Because it is free from defilements, it is pliant; because it is pliant, it is workable; because it is workable, it is steady;
because it is steady, it has reached imperturbability.
In this context, both stains and defilements belong to the side of craving.
Whatever wavering there is, and whatever instability of mind, this belongs to the side of views.
The four faculties—the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental grief, the faculty of pleasure, and the faculty of mental joy—cease in the fourth jhāna; for him, only the faculty of equanimity remains.
He attends to the higher attainment as peaceful, and as he so attends to the higher attainment as peaceful...
In the fourth jhāna, gross perception subsides, as does the perception of distress and the perception of resistance.
By completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity,
thinking "space is infinite," he realizes the attainment of the base of infinite space and, having entered upon it, dwells therein.
The application of direct knowledge transcends the perception of form, the perception of diversity, and the perception of resistance passes away for him;
thus, for one who is concentrated, the radiance and the vision of forms vanish from that concentration,
which is endowed with six factors and should be reviewed.
"My mind is accompanied by non-covetousness toward the entire world; my heart is free from ill will toward all beings;
my energy is aroused and exerted; my body is tranquil and unagitated; my mind is concentrated and undistracted;
my mindfulness is established and unconfused. In this regard, that mind which is accompanied by non-covetousness toward the entire world..."
That mind which is free from malice toward all beings, that energy which is aroused and exerted,
and that mind which is concentrated and undistracted— this is serenity (samatha).
That body which is tranquil and not agitated— this is the equipment for concentration (samādhiparikkhāra).
That mindfulness which is established and unconfused is insight.
That concentration is to be understood in five ways.
This concentration is "pleasant in the present"—thus its knowledge and vision is established within oneself.
This concentration "has a pleasant ripening in the future"—thus his personal knowledge and vision become manifest to him;
this concentration "is noble and spiritual"—thus his personal knowledge and vision become manifest to him;
this concentration "is practiced by superior men"—thus his personal knowledge and vision become manifest to him.

When this concentration exists, there arises in him a personal vision and knowledge that: "This concentration is peaceful and sublime, attained through tranquility, reached through unification, and is not something forced or restrained by volitional effort.
Furthermore, there arises in him a personal vision and knowledge that: "Mindfully I enter into this concentration, and mindfully I emerge from it."
In this regard, that concentration which is pleasant in the present and that concentration which has a pleasant result in the future—
this is serenity (*samatha*). That concentration which is noble and free from worldly taints, that concentration which is practiced by the great men, and that concentration which is peaceful,
sublime, attained through tranquility, reached through unification, and is not constrained by forced suppression or restraint— [this is insight (*vipassanā*)].
And as for the thought, "I enter this concentration mindfully and emerge from it mindfully," this is insight (*vipassanā*).
That concentration is to be understood in five ways: the pervasion of rapture, the pervasion of pleasure, the pervasion of the mind, the pervasion of light, and the sign of review.
Therein, that which is the pervasion of rapture, the pervasion of pleasure, and the pervasion of the mind—this is serenity (*samatha*).
That which is the pervasion of light and that which is the sign of reflection—this is insight (*vipassanā*).
The ten kasiṇa bases are: the earth kasiṇa, water kasiṇa, fire kasiṇa, air kasiṇa, blue kasiṇa, yellow kasiṇa, red kasiṇa, white kasiṇa, space kasiṇa, and consciousness kasiṇa.
In this context, the earth-kasina, the water-kasina, and likewise all [the others], as well as the white-kasina—
these eight kasinas are serenity (samatha).
That which is the space-kasina and the consciousness-kasina is insight (vipassanā).
In this way, the entire Noble Path, in whatever manner it has been described, should be applied to serenity and insight.
These are comprised by three things: impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
Developing serenity and insight, he develops the three gateways to liberation.
Cultivating the three gateways to liberation, one cultivates the three aggregates.
Cultivating the three aggregates, one cultivates the noble eightfold path.
A person of lustful temperament attains deliverance through the signless gateway to liberation while training in the higher training of the mind.
Abandoning the unwholesome root of greed, not approaching contact that is to be felt as pleasant,
fully understanding pleasant feeling, he washes away the stain of lust, shakes off the dust of lust, vomits out the poison of lust,
extinguishes the fire of lust, extracts the thorn of lust, and disentangles the tangle of lust.
A person whose temperament is dominated by hatred attains deliverance through the door of liberation that is the wishless (appaṇihita),
training in the higher training of virtue, abandoning the unwholesome root of hatred, not approaching contact that is to be experienced as painful,
fully understanding painful feeling, washing away the stain of hatred, shaking off the dust of hatred, vomiting out the poison of hatred, and extinguishing the fire of hatred.
Extinguishing the dart of hatred, uprooting the tangle of hatred, and disentangling the thicket of hatred;
a person of deluded temperament goes forth by means of the liberation-door of emptiness, training in the training of higher wisdom, abandoning the unwholesome root of delusion,
and avoiding contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, [attaining] neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

Fully understanding feeling, he washes away the stain of delusion, shakes off the dust of delusion, vomits up the poison of delusion, extinguishes the fire of delusion, extracts the thorn of delusion, and unravels the tangle of delusion.

In this context, the gateway to liberation that is emptiness is the aggregate of wisdom; the gateway to liberation that is signlessness is the aggregate of concentration; and the gateway to liberation that is wishlessness is the aggregate of virtue.
Thus, developing the three gateways to liberation, one develops the three aggregates; developing the three aggregates, one develops the noble eightfold path.
Therein, right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha);
right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration constitute the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha); and right view— [constitutes the aggregate of wisdom].
And that which is right intention is the aggregate of wisdom.
Therein, the aggregate of virtue and the aggregate of concentration are serenity; the aggregate of wisdom is insight.
For one who develops serenity and insight, two factors undergo development: body and mind. The way leading to the cessation of existence consists of two steps: virtue and concentration.
Thus a bhikkhu is one whose body is developed, whose virtue is developed, whose mind is developed, and whose wisdom is developed.
When the body is being developed, two qualities undergo development: right action and right effort.
When virtue is being developed, two qualities undergo development: right speech and right livelihood. When the mind is being developed...
Two factors come to fulfillment through development: right mindfulness and right concentration;
when wisdom is being developed, two factors come to fulfillment: right view and right intention.
In that regard, as for right action and right effort, they may be either bodily or mental. Therein, as for...
The restraint of body, when developed in the body, comes to fulfillment through development; the restraint of mind, when developed in the mind, comes to fulfillment through development.
Developing serenity and insight, he attains fivefold realization: he attains swift realization, realization of liberation, great realization, vast realization, and complete realization.

In that regard, through serenity (*samatha*), there is swift attainment, great attainment, and vast attainment; through insight (*vipassanā*), there is the attainment of liberation and the attainment of the remainderless.
In this context, the Teacher who teaches, endowed with the ten powers, does not deceive his disciples with his instruction.
He says: "Do this in three ways; do it by this means; for you who are doing this, it will lead to welfare and happiness."
It is impossible that one who has been thus exhorted and thus instructed, acting accordingly and practicing accordingly,

would fail to reach that plane. It is impossible that one who has been thus exhorted and thus instructed, while failing to fulfill the aggregate of virtuous conduct (*sīlakkhandha*), would reach that plane.
Thus, being thus exhorted and thus instructed, it is possible that he, fulfilling the aggregate of virtue, will reach that stage.
It is impossible that these things remain unawakened by you, who are a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
It is impossible that these taints remain undestroyed in you, whose all taints are utterly destroyed.
It is impossible that the Dhamma taught by you for a certain purpose would not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.

It is impossible that a disciple of yours who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, who practices correctly, and who lives according to the Dhamma, would not realize a successive, ever more sublime attainment.
It is impossible that those things which are obstacles, when indulged in, would not be sufficient to act as obstacles.
It is impossible that those teachings which do not lead out would lead one who practices them to the complete destruction of suffering;
it is possible that those teachings which do lead out would lead one who practices them to the complete destruction of suffering.
Furthermore, it is impossible that a disciple with a residue remaining would reach the Nibbāna-element without residue.
It is impossible for one endowed with right view to deprive his mother of life or to kill her easily with his own hands or feet;
it is possible for an ordinary person (puthujjana) to deprive his mother of life or to kill her easily with his own hands or feet.

In this way, it is impossible for a person accomplished in view to split the Saṅgha or create a schism in the Saṅgha; but it is possible for an ordinary person to split the Saṅgha or create a schism in the Saṅgha. It is impossible for one who has committed an offense to be purified by confessing that offense before an individual, an arahant, a bhikkhu, his father, or the Saṅgha; but it is possible for one who has committed an offense to be purified by confessing that offense before an ordinary person. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to commit an offense that is an immediate transgression; but it is possible for an ordinary person to commit an offense that is an immediate transgression. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of afflicted spirits; but it is possible for an ordinary person to be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of afflicted spirits. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to undergo an intermediate existence; but it is possible for an ordinary person to undergo an intermediate existence. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die with a mind that is not concentrated; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die with a mind that is not concentrated. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to birth; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to birth. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to old age; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to old age. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to illness; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to illness. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to hunger and thirst; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to hunger and thirst. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to cold and heat; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to cold and heat. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to fear; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to fear. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to lamentation; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to lamentation. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to despair; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to despair. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five lower fetters; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five lower fetters. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five higher fetters; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five higher fetters. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five bonds; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five bonds. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five obstructions; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five obstructions. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five hindrances; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five hindrances. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five defilements; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five defilements. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five stains; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five stains. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five corruptions; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five corruptions. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five attachments; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five attachments. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five cravings; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five cravings. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five clingings; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five clingings. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five obsessions; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five obsessions. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five bondages; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five bondages. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five shackles; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five shackles. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five fetters; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five fetters. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five ties; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five ties. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five obscurations; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five obscurations. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five coverings; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five coverings. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five veils; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five veils. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five shrouds; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five shrouds. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five obsessions; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five obsessions. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five bondages; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five bondages. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five shackles; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five shackles. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five fetters; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five fetters. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five ties; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five ties. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five obscurations; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five obscurations. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five coverings; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five coverings. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five veils; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five veils. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five shrouds; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five shrouds. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five obsessions; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five obsessions. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five ties; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five ties. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five obscurations; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five obscurations. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five coverings; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five coverings. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five veils; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die while still subject to the five veils. It is impossible for a person accomplished in view to die while still subject to the five shrouds; but it is possible for an ordinary person to die

It is impossible that one endowed with right view would, with a mind of hatred, draw blood from a Tathāgata, or that one would, with a mind of hatred, destroy the stupa of a Tathāgata who has attained final Nibbāna; such a thing cannot happen.

It is possible that an ordinary person (puthujjana), with a mind of hatred, would draw blood from a Tathāgata, or that one would, with a mind of hatred, destroy the stupa of a Tathāgata who has attained final Nibbāna; such a thing can happen.
It is impossible that one who is accomplished in view would, even for the sake of his life, acknowledge another teacher; it is possible that an ordinary person might acknowledge another teacher.
It is impossible that one who is accomplished in view would seek outside of this [Dhamma] for another worthy of offerings;
it is possible that an ordinary person might seek outside of this for another worthy of offerings. One who is accomplished in view...
That an ordinary person might attain purity through curiosity and auspicious rites—this is impossible.
That a woman might be a wheel-turning monarch—this is impossible. That a man might be a wheel-turning monarch—this is possible.
That a woman might become Sakka, lord of the devas—this is impossible; that a man might become Sakka, lord of the devas—this is possible.
That a woman might become Māra the Evil One—this is impossible; that a man might become Māra the Evil One—this is possible.
That a woman might become Mahābrahmā—this is impossible; that a man might become Mahābrahmā—this is possible.
That a female might be a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One—this is impossible; that a male might be a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One—this is possible.

That two Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones should arise or teach the Dharma simultaneously in a single world-system—this is impossible; only one Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One [can do so].
It is possible that one [Buddha] will arise in a single world-system or will teach the Dhamma;

this is a possibility. That the result of the three types of misconduct will be desirable, attractive, pleasant, and agreeable—this is impossible. That the result of the three types of misconduct will be undesirable, unattractive, unpleasant, and disagreeable—this is possible.

It is impossible that the result of the three kinds of good conduct will be undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, or disagreeable; it is possible that the result of the three kinds of good conduct will be desirable, lovely, pleasant, and agreeable.

Yet some ascetic or brahmin—a deceiver, a talker, a soothsayer—making deception, talkativeness, and fortune-telling his primary concern, fails to abandon the five hindrances, those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom.
It is impossible that one who dwells with mindfulness unestablished in the four foundations of mindfulness, and who has not cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment,
should awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; unless, indeed, some ascetic or brahmin,
free from all faults, having abandoned the five hindrances— those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom— [should do so].

"It is possible that one who dwells with mindfulness established in the four foundations of mindfulness, having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, will awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment"—this is a possibility.
The knowledge regarding this, in terms of cause and in terms of possibility, without limitation, is called the first power of the Tathāgata: the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible.

Thus, all things pertaining to what is possible and impossible are subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation; some go to heaven, some go to the states of misery, and some go to Nibbāna. Thus the Blessed One said:
"All beings will die, for life ends in death."
They will go according to their deeds,
receiving the fruits of merit and evil;
those of evil karma will go to hell.
And those with meritorious deeds go to a good destination;
others, having developed the path,
attain final Nibbāna, free from taints.
"All beings" refers to both the noble ones and the non-noble ones, those included within the sphere of self-identity (*sakkāya*) and those who have transcended self-identity.
"Will die" means by two kinds of death: slow death and quick death; for those included within self-identity it is quick death, while for those who have transcended self-identity it is slow death.
"Life ends in death" means that with the exhaustion of the life-span and the cessation of the faculties, there is the limit of life and the limit of death.
“They will go according to their karma” refers to the ownership of one’s actions (*kammassakatā*).
“Experiencing the fruits of merit and evil” refers both to the visibility of the results of actions and to their inseparability from those results.
“Those of evil deeds [go] to hell” refers to unwholesome volitional formations (*apuñña-saṅkhāra*).
"And those of meritorious deeds go to a happy destination": those who have formed volitional formations of merit will go to a good rebirth.
And others, having developed the path, "attain final Nibbāna, free from taints": this refers to the complete transcending of all formations.
Thus the Blessed One said.
“All beings... [as above] ...are without taints.
“All beings will die; for life ends in death.”
“They will go according to their karma, experiencing the fruits of merit and evil;
those of evil deeds go to hell”—this is the harsh and agonizing way.
“Others, having developed the path, attain final Nibbāna with the taints destroyed”—this is the middle way.
“All beings will die; for life has death as its end. They will go according to their karma, receiving the fruits of merit and evil; those of evil deeds [go] to hell”—this is corruption (*saṅkilesa*).
In this way, one brings about *saṃsāra*.
“All beings will die …pe…” [and so on].
“Those of evil deeds go to hell”—these are the three rounds: the round of suffering, the round of kamma, and the round of defilements.
“And others, having developed the path, attain final Nibbāna, their taints destroyed”—this is the turning away from the three rounds.
“All beings will die …” [and so on].

"Those of evil deeds go to hell" is the disadvantage (*ādīnava*); "those of meritorious deeds go to a happy destination" is the gratification (*assāda*); and "others, having developed the path, attain final Nibbāna, free from taints" is the escape (*nissaraṇa*).

In the passage, "All beings will die... those of evil deeds go to hell," there is both cause and fruit: the five aggregates are the fruit, and craving is the cause. In the passage, "Others, having developed the path, attain final Nibbāna, free from taints," there is both the path and the fruit.
“All beings will die, for life ends in death.

According to their karma they will go, reaping the fruits of merit and evil; those of evil deeds go to hell. This is corruption. That corruption is threefold: the corruption of craving, the corruption of views, and the corruption of misconduct.
Therein, the corruption of craving is to be demonstrated by means of the three types of craving.
[It is] craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
Or else, it should be demonstrated by whichever specific object one is attached to; its detailed exposition consists of the thirty-six courses of the net-like craving.
Therein, the corruption of views is to be demonstrated by way of annihilationism and eternalism, or by whichever specific object [one holds].
One adheres by way of views, thinking, "This alone is the truth; anything else is false," and it is to be demonstrated by means of this or that [view].
Its detailed exposition consists of the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*).

Therein, the corruption of misconduct is to be demonstrated by volition and mental action (*cetasika-kamma*), namely, by the three types of misconduct: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. Its detailed exposition consists of the ten unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kammapatha*).
And others, having developed the path, attain final Nibbāna with the destruction of the taints—this is the cleansing.
This cleansing is threefold:
the defilement of craving is purified by serenity; that serenity is the aggregate of concentration; [and] the defilement of views...
One is purified by insight; that insight is the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*). Defilement through misconduct is purified by good conduct;
that good conduct is the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).
"All beings will die, for life ends in death; they will go according to their karma, reaping the fruits of merit and evil."
"Those of evil deeds go to hell" is the practice of demerit; "those of meritorious deeds go to a happy destination" is the practice of merit;
and "others, having developed the path, attain final nibbāna with the taints destroyed" is the practice that transcends both merit and demerit.
In this context, both the practice of merit and the practice of demerit constitute one single practice leading everywhere.
In the states of misery there is one [path], among the devas there is one, and that which is the practice for transcending both merit and demerit is the path leading to various destinations.
There are three groups:
the group fixed in falsehood, the group fixed in truth, and the group not fixed; therein, that which is fixed in falsehood...
The group that is fixed in rightness is the single path leading to each respective destination;
therein, the group that is unfixed is the path leading everywhere.
For what reason?
If he were to obtain the requisite conditions, he might be reborn in hell; if he were to obtain the requisite conditions, he might be reborn among the animal realm;
if he were to obtain the requisite conditions, he might be reborn in the sphere of hungry ghosts; if he were to obtain the requisite conditions, he might be reborn among the asuras;

if he were to obtain the requisite conditions, he might be reborn among the devas; if he were to obtain the requisite conditions, he might be reborn among human beings. If he were to obtain the requisite conditions...
If one were to attain [the goal] while still living, one would then attain final Nibbāna; therefore, this is the practice leading everywhere.
That knowledge therein, which is according to cause and according to condition, without limitation—this is called the knowledge of the practice leading everywhere, the second power of a Tathāgata.
Thus, the world of many elements is the practice leading everywhere; the world of various elements is the practice leading here and there.
In this regard, what is the world of many elements?
It is the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element.
The body element, the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element; the mind element, the mental-phenomena element, the mind-consciousness element;
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element;
the sense-desire element, the ill-will element, the cruelty element, the renunciation element, the non-ill-will element, the non-cruelty element, and the suffering element.
The element of displeasure, the element of ignorance, the element of pleasure, the element of joy, the element of equanimity, the element of form, the element of the formless,
the element of cessation, the element of formations, and the element of Nibbāna— this is the world of many elements. In this context,
what is the world of diverse elements?
The eye-element is one thing, the form-element is another, the eye-consciousness-element is another; so it is for all [the eighteen elements], and the element of Nibbāna is yet another.
That knowledge herein which is according to cause, according to basis, and without limitation—this is called the third Tathāgata-power, the knowledge of the manifold elements and diverse elements.
Thus, regarding this world of manifold and diverse elements, whatever element beings are inclined toward, that very same [element]...

They resolve and they adhere: some are intent upon forms, some are intent upon sounds, some are intent upon odors, some are intent upon tastes, some are intent upon tangibles, some are intent upon mental phenomena;
some are intent upon women, some are intent upon men, some are intent upon generosity, some are intent upon the inferior, and some are intent upon the sublime.
Some are resolved upon the devas, some are resolved upon human beings, and some are resolved upon Nibbāna.

That knowledge which, according to cause and according to ground, is unrestricted—knowing "this one is to be disciplined," "this one is not to be disciplined," "this one is bound for heaven," and "this one is bound for a state of misery"—this is called the knowledge of the diversity of inclinations among beings, the fourth power of a Tathāgata.
Thus they are as they are inclined, and they undertake various undertakings of kamma.
They undertake that sixfold action:
some out of greed, some out of hatred, some out of delusion, some out of faith, some out of energy, and some out of wisdom.
When analyzed, it is twofold.
It leads both to saṃsāra and to nibbāna.
In this regard, whatever kamma one performs through greed, hatred, and delusion, this kamma is black with black result.
In this regard, whatever kamma one performs through faith, this kamma is white with white result.
In this regard, whatever action one performs through greed, hatred, delusion, and faith, this action is black-and-white with black-and-white result.

In this regard, whatever action one performs through energy and wisdom, this action is neither-black-nor-white with neither-black-nor-white result; it is the supreme action, the best action, which leads to the destruction of action.
There are four ways of undertaking action:
There is an undertaking of action that is pleasant in the present but has a painful ripening in the future;
there is an undertaking of action that is painful in the present but has a pleasant ripening in the future;

there is an undertaking of action that is painful both in the present and has a painful ripening in the future; and there is an undertaking of action that is pleasant both in the present and has a pleasant ripening in the future.

Regarding such a course of action undertaken in this life, the Blessed One does not advise that person who has accumulated an unwholesome undertaking of action that has not yet ripened but is present for its result, and who is incapable of reaching liberation.
This is as in the case of Devadatta, Kokālika, Sunakkhatta the son of the Licchavis, or whatever other beings are fixed in falsehood;
and regarding the unwholesome accumulated by these persons which has not yet reached completion, but will reach completion before long.

The Blessed One gives instruction to those who are unequal because [the unwholesome action] will produce its fruit before [the Path], will obstruct the Path before [it can arise], and will cause one to transcend the state of being a fit vessel for training before [the Path can take hold].
This is like the case of Puṇṇa the cow-tender and Acela the dog-votary.
For this person, the undertaking of unwholesome kamma, while reaching completion, will obstruct the Path before [it can arise].

The Blessed One gives this incomparable advice because [the person] is reaching completion, before the fruit can arise, before the path can be obstructed, and before they transcend the state of being a fit vessel for training—
just as he did with the Venerable Aṅgulimāla.

The mild, medium, and intense degrees of all [formative activities]. Therein, the formative activities of the imperturbable (*āneñja*) are mild; the remaining wholesome formative activities are medium; and unwholesome formative activities are intense.

That knowledge herein which is specific as to cause and as to occasion—namely, "this is to be experienced in the present life" and "this is to be experienced upon rebirth"—is [the knowledge of the result of kamma].
"This is to be experienced in subsequent lives; this is to be experienced in hell; this is to be experienced in the animal realm; this is to be experienced in the sphere of hungry ghosts;

this is to be experienced among the asuras; this is to be experienced among the devas; this is to be experienced among human beings"—this is called the fifth Tathāgata-power, the knowledge of the diversity of the ripening of undertakings of kamma according to their causes, according to their bases, and without exception regarding the past, future, and present.
Thus, regarding those kamma-formations undertaken, those jhānas undertaken, those liberations, concentrations, and attainments, there is unobstructed knowledge:
"This is their corruption, this is their cleansing, this is their emergence; thus it becomes corrupted, thus it is cleansed, thus it emerges."
In that regard, how many jhānas are there?
There are four jhānas.
How many liberations (vimokkhas) are there?
Eleven, eight, seven, three, and two.
How many kinds of concentration are there?
There are three kinds of concentration:
Concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only; concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought.
How many attainments are there?
There are five attainments:

The attainment of perception, the attainment of non-perception, the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the attainment of the fading away of perception, and the attainment of cessation.
In this context, what is defilement?
For the first jhāna, sensual desire and ill will are the defilements.
The two initial "cock-like" meditations (*kukkuṭajhāyī*) and whatever concentration partakes of decline—this is corruption (*saṅkileso*).

In this context, what is purification (*vodāna*)? The purity from hindrances (*nīvaraṇapārisuddhi*), the two final "cock-like" meditations of the first *jhāna*, and whatever concentration partakes of distinction—this is purification.
In this context, what is emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*)?
Skill in emerging from attainment is emergence.

The knowledge therein, which is comprehensive regarding the cause and the ground, is called the sixth Tathāgata-power: the knowledge of the defilement, cleansing, and emergence of all jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
Thus, for that very concentration, there are three accompanying factors: the faculties, the powers, and energy; these indeed—
The faculties become powers by way of energy: they are faculties in the sense of dominance, and powers in the sense of being unshakable.
Thus, according to their mildness, mediocrity, or intensity, there is "one of dull faculties," "one of moderate faculties," and "one of sharp faculties.

In this regard, the Blessed One exhorts one of sharp faculties with a brief exhortation; the Blessed One exhorts one of moderate faculties with both brief and detailed exhortations; and the Blessed One exhorts one of dull faculties with a detailed exhortation.

In that regard, the Blessed One teaches a gentle Dhamma-discourse to one with sharp faculties; the Blessed One teaches a discourse on both gentle and sharp Dhamma to one with medium faculties; the Blessed One teaches a sharp Dhamma-discourse to one with dull faculties.

In that regard, the Blessed One teaches tranquility (samatha) to one with sharp faculties; the Blessed One teaches both tranquility and insight (vipassanā) to one with medium faculties; the Blessed One teaches insight to one with dull faculties.

In that regard, the Blessed One points out the escape for one with sharp faculties; for one with medium faculties, the Blessed One points out both the danger and the escape; for one with dull faculties, the Blessed One points out the gratification, the danger, and the escape.

In that regard, the Blessed One establishes one with sharp faculties in the training of higher wisdom; the Blessed One establishes one with medium faculties in the training of higher mind; the Blessed One establishes one with dull faculties in the training of higher virtue.
The knowledge therein regarding the cause and the ground without limitation— that this person has reached this stage and this development;
that at this time and by this instruction, such is his constituent elements, such his disposition, and such his underlying tendency— this is called the seventh Tathāgata-power,
the knowledge of the diversity in the faculties of other beings and other persons.
Thus, therein, he recollects his manifold past abodes;
that is to say:
one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births...
Twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births;
many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, many hundreds of thousands of births;
many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion.
"In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I arose elsewhere.
There too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.

In this regard, among beings who have gone to heaven, those who have gone to the human realm, and those who have gone to the states of woe, for this person greed and so forth are predominant while non-greed and so forth are weak;
for this other person, non-greed and so forth are predominant while greed and so forth are weak;
or else, whichever are predominant and whichever are weak, these are the faculties of this person.
"These faculties of this person have been accumulated; those [other] faculties have not been accumulated for such-and-such a ten-million-eon period,
or a hundred thousand eons, or a thousand eons, or a hundred eons, or an eon, or an intermediate eon, or half an eon, or a year,
or half a year, or a month, or a fortnight, or a day, or a moment— due to this negligence or this lack of confidence."

Recalling each such existence, the Blessed One knows it without exception; therein, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma:
"Alas, these worthy beings, through misconduct of body..."
Endowed with misconduct of speech, endowed with misconduct of mind, revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong views,
and undertaking actions based on wrong views, they— upon the breakup of the body, after death— were reborn in a state of deprivation,
a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these worthy beings, who were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind;

who did not revile the noble ones, who held right view, and undertook actions based on right view—upon the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world, among those beings who have gone to heaven or who have reached the human state. Among those beings who have gone to heaven...
And among beings who have fallen into the states of misery, this person has accumulated such karma for a certain number of ten million aeons,
or a hundred thousand aeons, or a thousand aeons, or a hundred aeons, or an intermediate aeon, or half an aeon,
or a year, or half a year, or a month, or a fortnight, or a day.
"Either for a moment, or by this negligence, or by this confidence.
These are two knowledges of the Blessed One—
the knowledge of recollecting past lives and the divine eye— which are the eighth and ninth powers of a Tathāgata.

Thus, therein, that all-knowingness which has been attained, the knowledge of all phenomena that is dustless and stainless, the omniscient knowledge that has arisen, and Māra who was struck down at the foot of the Bodhi tree—this is the tenth power of the Blessed One, the knowledge of the total destruction of all taints (*āsava*).
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are endowed with these ten powers.
The section on the "Method of Investigation" (*vicayahārasampāta*) is concluded.
